name: Photo-based item logging
shortDesc: Take a photo → AI auto-tags the object + its location context.
description: The core capture loop. The patient or caregiver raises the phone, takes a photo, and the app tags what's in the frame ("reading glasses", "hearing aids") plus the spatial context ("kitchen counter"). This is the foundational input that powers search, reminders, and caregiver visibility. Without this, ReCall has no reason to exist.
voicedBy: Margaret, Robert, Elena, PRD core feature
designNotes: One tap from home screen or widget. No confirmation dialogs. Offline-capable with sync on reconnect. Image compression before upload. Graceful degradation when AI tag confidence is low — offer user-typed fallback.

name: Natural-language search
shortDesc: "Where are my glasses?" returns photo + location + time last seen.
description: The other half of the core product. Margaret asks a plain-language question — spoken or typed — and gets back the photo, the location it was logged at, and when. This is the retrieval side of the capture+search loop. Natural language matters because typed commands are high-friction for this user.
designNotes: Result in under 2 seconds or it feels broken. Always show the photo, not just text. Show timestamp context ("yesterday morning") in human-friendly form. Failure mode: graceful "no match" + list of recent items.

name: Repeated-query tolerance
shortDesc: Ask the same thing 50 times, get the same calm answer 50 times.
description: Dementia means asking the same question repeatedly. Any app that says "you already asked" — or even subtly signals that it noticed — will be abandoned. This feature is the absence of a feature: no counters, no nudges, no escalation. It's a product principle enforced as a testable requirement.
designNotes: Testable: run the same query 30 times in 10 minutes; every response must be identical in tone, format, and latency. No behavioral analytics surface the repetition to the user.

name: Calm, non-alarming UI
shortDesc: No reds. No urgency. No alarms. Warm, steady, unchanging.
description: This population has anxiety as a co-symptom. Red backgrounds, flashing icons, urgency indicators, or even bold call-to-action buttons can trigger panic. Every visual decision — palette, type weight, animation — is tuned for the most anxious user (Linda).
designNotes: Warm-neutral palette. Avoid pure red even for errors — use amber or brown instead. No motion animations longer than 150ms. No sounds by default; optional soft chimes.

name: One-tap confirm on save
shortDesc: Save an item in a single tap. No multi-step wizards.
description: Cognitive load budget is near zero. A two-step save — take a photo, then tap "Done" — already pushes some patients out. The save action must be one tap, with an optional tap to correct before auto-confirm. Multi-step flows are acceptable for less-frequent actions, never for capture.
designNotes: Auto-save after 3-second pause if no edit. "Fix" button always visible. No confirmation dialogs.

name: Always correctable
shortDesc: User (or caregiver) can always fix an AI label or location.
description: AI will make mistakes. If the user can't fix "this is a remote" when it's actually a hearing aid case, trust evaporates and usage stops. Every AI-generated label, location, and tag must have a visible correction path. This is also how the app gets smarter per-user over time.
designNotes: Edit path is always one tap from the item detail view. Corrections are persisted and inform future AI suggestions. No shaming ("Sorry, I got that wrong") — neutral acknowledgement only.

name: Basic time/day orientation
shortDesc: "It's 3:15pm on Wednesday afternoon" — always visible.
description: Many patients cannot reliably answer "what day is it?" This is a foundational context anchor — the first thing shown on the home screen. Format matters: 3:15 PM Wednesday is confusing; "Wednesday afternoon, about 3:15" is clearer.
designNotes: Conversational format ("morning", "afternoon", "evening"). Large type. Always on home. Never collapsed. Culturally localizable (not everyone uses 12-hour clock).

name: Caregiver logging mode
shortDesc: Caregiver/family can log items on patient's behalf.
description: Many patients — James, Harold — won't or can't drive the app themselves. If caregiver logging isn't a first-class mode, the app only works for the highest-functioning 20% of the target population. This is distinct from multi-device: even on one device, there must be a clear "I'm logging for someone else" flow.
designNotes: Caregiver view is slightly different from patient view — adds notes field, bulk logging. Handoff between views is a single tap. Never surface caregiver notes to patient by default.

name: Multi-device architecture
shortDesc: Each person uses their OWN device; data syncs to a shared patient profile.
description: Priya logs from her phone 2000 miles away. Robert logs from his own iPhone in the same kitchen. Elena uses her own Android during shifts. The app is inherently a multi-user, multi-device system — single-device architecture forces everyone to share the patient's phone, which defeats the caregiver use case. See: Multi-Device Architecture Decision Memo (April 16, 2026).
voicedBy: Priya, Robert, Elena (panel); PRD Family View (implied)
designNotes: Firebase Firestore + anonymous auth. Invitation via short code. MVP supports Patient + Caregiver roles; facility and multi-patient deferred to Phase 3. Offline-first with optimistic writes.

name: AI object recognition accuracy
shortDesc: How often the AI correctly labels an object on first try.
description: The better this is, the less the user has to correct, which means less friction and more trust. 95%+ first-try accuracy feels magical; 60% accuracy feels constant-correction-exhausting and eventually drives abandonment. Budget real engineering time for model selection, fine-tuning on household objects, and edge cases (pill bottles, keys at distance, glasses).
designNotes: Track first-try accuracy as a product-health metric. Fall back to user-typed label below confidence threshold. Personalize over time from user corrections.

name: Voice input quality
shortDesc: Speech-to-text reliability for capture, search, and reminders.
description: Voice is central to ReCall — "I'm putting her hearing aids on the bathroom counter" needs to work first try. A failed voice transcription sends the user back to typing, which many won't do. Regional accents, softer voices, and household noise are all real-world conditions to design against.
designNotes: Use platform-native speech APIs (iOS Speech, Web Speech) first; consider Whisper API as fallback for accuracy. Visible transcript before commit. Easy re-record path.

name: Search result speed
shortDesc: Time from query to answer.
description: Sub-2-second responses feel reassuring. Over 5 seconds creates anxiety — the patient starts wondering if they did something wrong, if the app is broken, or if the answer is bad news. This is a measured metric, not a vibe: instrument it and hold a target.
designNotes: P50 < 1s, P95 < 2.5s. Show a calm skeleton state rather than a spinner. Local-first cache for recent queries.

name: Morning briefing relevance
shortDesc: What the app shows on the home screen first thing in the morning.
description: The first thing patient or caregiver sees each day: date, day-part, appointments, medication status, recent items. Done well it's a trusted daily anchor. Done badly (too much, too little, irrelevant) it becomes background noise and gets ignored. This is where the app earns or loses daily engagement.
designNotes: Max 5 tiles. Prioritize by recency and criticality. Never show overdue items with red — use warm amber instead. Customizable per user by caregiver.

name: Semantic location suggestions
shortDesc: Locations learned from usage ("kitchen counter", "bedroom drawer").
description: Unique to ReCall vs. generic photo apps: the system learns user-defined locations over time and suggests previously-used ones during capture, so logging "glasses → bedroom drawer" the second time is one tap instead of retyping. No GPS, no mapping — just human-language places that become faster as the system learns.
designNotes: Top-5 suggested locations based on recency + frequency. Free-text fallback always available. Patient can rename locations globally.

name: Medication photo confirmation
shortDesc: Photo of empty pill slot = visual proof of intake.
description: Dose tracking via photo beats checkbox UI for this population — a photo is tamper-obvious evidence that the pill was actually taken. Remote family sees visual proof, not a self-reported tap. This is the dignity-forward alternative to "did you take your pill?" nagging.
designNotes: Detect empty slot via AI; verify against time-of-day. Store photo encrypted. Missed-dose alert if photo not taken within caregiver-set window.

name: Safety check photo recall
shortDesc: Find "did I lock the door?" photo quickly at 2am.
description: Linda wakes at 2am worrying about the stove. A pre-captured photo of the stove-off dial, retrievable in two taps from the lock screen, ends the anxiety. Speed matters more than anything else — if she has to unlock the phone, navigate, and wait, she's awake for the night.
designNotes: Lock-screen widget for last-checked items. Photo must load in under 1 second. Optional: voice-activated recall ("Show me stove").

name: Caregiver status view
shortDesc: At-a-glance "how is Mom doing today?" for remote family.
description: The single screen Priya looks at each morning: green/yellow/red on key indicators (medication taken, safety checks done, recent activity). High-signal, low-noise — not a log, not a dashboard, just the answer to "do I need to be worried?"
designNotes: Three colors, never more. Tap any indicator for detail. No push notifications from this view — it's a pull experience.

name: Nightly safety screen
shortDesc: 4-item bedtime confirmation: door, stove, meds, alarm.
description: A dedicated bedtime view that shows four checked-off items with their confirmation photos. Accessed with one tap from the home screen (or automatically at a user-set hour). Linda goes to sleep without re-checking the kitchen. This is a small feature with an outsized emotional payoff — a key delighter moment.
designNotes: Show photo thumbnails, not just labels. Timestamp on each. "Tap to check again" path that doesn't require re-capturing.

name: Caregiver-driven origination
shortDesc: Family organizes items for patient; patient benefits invisibly.
description: Priya organizes her dad's common items while visiting over the holidays. When she leaves, he can find everything — without ever being told the system exists or having to learn it. This is the "invisible is better than helpful" principle in action, and it unlocks patients (Harold) who would otherwise refuse the app.
designNotes: Caregiver-logged items have no visual distinction on patient side. Caregiver can see their own vs. patient-created items in caregiver view only.

name: Contextual time hints
shortDesc: "Last seen yesterday morning" alongside photo result.
description: When the app returns a search result, it tags it with a human-friendly time context ("last seen yesterday morning") rather than a raw timestamp. This helps the user reconstruct their own timeline, which is itself a cognitive aid — and makes the app feel smart and caring rather than dumb and logging.
designNotes: Fuzzy time labels ("yesterday morning", "a few minutes ago", "earlier this week"). Hover/long-press for exact timestamp.

name: Structured usage logging (silent)
shortDesc: Every interaction is logged to a research-grade schema from day one.
description: Invisible to the patient, this data layer captures every query, every capture, every correction with timestamps, categories, and results. Day one it enables the research angle (Dr. Carter), clinical correlation (Dr. Rosenfeld), and future product tuning. Architectural rather than UI-visible — but architecturally the most important decision.
designNotes: Opt-in for anonymized export. Never surfaces as a number back to the patient (no streaks, no counts). Schema is stable from MVP onward.

name: Morning voice briefing
shortDesc: "Good morning, Linda. Today is Wednesday. Dentist at 2pm."
description: A calm, warm voice reads the morning briefing aloud. Linda never expected this — and when it happens, it feels like having a gentle companion. Emotionally this is one of the strongest hooks the app can deliver. Fast-follow after MVP because voice synthesis quality matters a lot and shouldn't be rushed.
designNotes: User selects voice from 2–3 options (avoid uncanny valley). Pauses naturally. Never chirpy. Triggered by user opening app in the morning, not pushed.

name: Voice self-reminders
shortDesc: Record a reminder in your own voice; hear yourself later.
description: Margaret records "Call the dentist tomorrow" in her own voice. The next day, the app plays it back to her in her own voice. Her voice = her intent, which is trust-forward for dementia patients who may distrust automated prompts. Extends voice from input to self-directed memory tool.
designNotes: Pair each reminder with an optional photo (dentist's card). Caregiver can see pending reminders. Never play back unless user opened the app (no surprise audio).

name: Voice feedback synthesis
shortDesc: Patient voices daily challenges; system synthesizes for caregivers.
description: Margaret complains aloud "I can never find the damn remote in the evening." The app captures this, doesn't do anything obtrusive, but synthesizes it into caregiver insights ("Patient struggles with TV remote in evenings — consider a dedicated spot"). Closes the loop between lived experience and caregiver support.
designNotes: Requires explicit opt-in ("let the app listen for frustrations"). NEVER raw audio to caregivers — synthesis only. Daily or weekly digest cadence.

name: Scaffolded Active Recall (NEW)
shortDesc: Four-stage retrieval: free recall → cued → recognition (MC) → answer.
description: Before showing the answer, the app invites the patient to try to remember. If they can't, it offers a cue. Still stuck, it offers 3–4 multiple-choice locations (all real places from recent history). Finally, it shows the photo. This walks the patient down the cognitive-neuroscience retrieval ladder (free recall → cued → recognition), exercising the weakest function first. Optional, opt-in, skippable at every stage. See Addendum Part 6 in the Unified Needs doc.
voicedBy: Dr. Lauren Kim (panel), enhanced by Ravster
designNotes: Opt-in per-patient (caregiver or OT sets). One persistent "Just show me" escape. No gamification. Distractors are REAL locations from history. Quietly feeds retrieval-stage data into the research pipeline.

name: Ambient display mode
shortDesc: Kitchen screen passively showing recent item locations. No interaction.
description: Harold refuses to use a phone. But a tablet mounted on the kitchen counter showing "Keys: hook. Wallet: dresser. Hearing aids: bedside." — he'd glance at it. This is an entirely different form factor that unlocks the tech-resistant persona. Revolutionary for that segment.
designNotes: Rotates through most-searched items. No tap targets. Screen-saver mode. Low-brightness default. Pairs with existing patient profile over Wi-Fi.

name: Person identification (manual)
shortDesc: "Who was that woman who came to dinner?" via photo + timestamp.
description: Margaret can't remember the woman who visited Tuesday but she remembers the visit. The app lets her browse photos from that day — each tagged with who it is (manually entered by caregiver during visit, or post-hoc). Preserves social memory, which is deeply emotional territory. Manual tagging first; facial recognition only in Phase 3+ with strong consent.
designNotes: Tagged by caregiver; surfaced to patient. Relationship context ("this is Jane, your sister's daughter"). Never auto-suggest names without confirmation.

name: De-escalation notes
shortDesc: Patient-specific calming strategies, instantly accessible.
description: Marcus starts a night shift at 11pm. A patient is sundowning, agitated. He pulls up de-escalation notes: "Plays Sinatra. Mentions her late husband's name. Weighted blanket on the chair." Collected by family and prior caregivers over time. Night-shift game-changer.
designNotes: Always accessible from lock screen in caregiver mode. Short, scannable bullet format. Caregiver can add notes without waking patient (silent capture).

name: Pill identification via camera
shortDesc: Camera reads pill imprint to confirm correct medication.
description: Patient or caregiver holds a pill up to the camera. The app reads the imprint code, matches it against the prescribed list, and confirms "Yes, that's your blood-pressure pill" before ingestion. Safety + peace-of-mind for remote family. Regulatory complexity makes this Phase 3 — needs FDA-aware legal review.
designNotes: Requires external pill-imprint database license. Requires medical-device-adjacent disclaimers. Never blocks ingestion — advises only. Opt-in.

name: Caregiver burnout detection
shortDesc: Passive signal when caregiver interaction patterns show stress.
description: Dr. Rosenfeld identified caregiver burnout as the #1 predictor of patient crisis. Usage patterns — logging frequency, help requests, time-of-day — can reveal when the caregiver is struggling. The app can offer "someone noticed you seem stretched, here are resources" without judging or demanding action.
designNotes: Never call it "burnout" in UI. Opt-in detection. Resources sourced from Alzheimer's Association. Privacy: caregiver controls whether this signal is visible to family.

name: Clinical correlation
shortDesc: App usage patterns ↔ formal cognitive scores (MMSE, MoCA).
description: Dr. Carter wants to correlate ReCall usage patterns with standardized cognitive assessments. If search-frequency + retrieval-stage (from Active Recall) map to MMSE decline, ReCall becomes a real-world cognitive biomarker. This is the research angle's endgame — publishable, defensible, category-defining.
designNotes: Requires consented research cohort. IRB review needed. Partnership with an academic neuropsych lab. Long timeline but high-strategic-value deliverable.

name: Mood tracker with trend chart
shortDesc: Once-a-day mood tap (emoji or 1–10 scale) graphed over time for caregivers.
description: A lightweight daily mood check-in for the patient — five faces, or a 1-to-10 scale — captured in one tap. Values are graphed over weeks and months in the caregiver-status view, giving Priya and Dr. Rosenfeld a quantitative early-warning signal that's complementary to the voice-feedback synthesis feature. Inspired by Recollect (Mythos Foundation), which bundles mood with medication and memory. Done well, the trend line is what families will consciously compare between products.
voicedBy: Competitive analysis (Recollect); reinforces Dr. Carter's structured-data need and Priya's remote-status view
designNotes: Must be skippable without guilt. No streaks (Reverse guidance). Graph uses calm palette, not red for low days. Clinician-facing export if research consent given. Consider prompting at morning briefing so it lives in an existing habit.

name: Picture phonebook
shortDesc: Large-face contact list — tap a face to call.
description: Margaret wants to call her daughter but can't remember her name in order to search. The picture phonebook surfaces the important people in her life as oversized face photos, each with name + relationship + last-contact context. One tap places the call (or starts a video chat, via platform handoff). Distinct from Person Identification, which is reactive ("who was that?"); this is a proactive communication aid inspired by Timeless. An emotionally resonant delighter at low engineering cost once the photo vault and person-tagging exist.
designNotes: Ordered by recency + frequency of contact. Caregiver curates the list. No badge counts, no "missed call" guilt. Tap placement calls via native dialer/FaceTime/WhatsApp — don't build our own telephony.

name: Localization (Spanish first, then more)
shortDesc: Native-language UI + voice for non-English households.
description: Our backlog is English-only. Roughly 13% of US adults over 65 speak primarily Spanish at home, and that population is under-served by every dementia app we reviewed except My ALZ Journey. Native-language UI strings, voice synthesis, and speech-to-text is linearly better the more languages are supported. Spanish first because market size and resource availability; add based on user-research findings. For a Spanish-speaking Margaret, this is Must-Be, not Performance — so it may be worth elevating at the MVP+ stage depending on pilot cohort.
voicedBy: Competitive analysis (My ALZ Journey); inclusivity principle from Tanya
designNotes: Centralized copy system from day one of MVP so retrofit is string-file, not rewrite. Professional translation with dementia-domain review (not raw LLM translation). Voice synthesis must use native-speaker voices, not accented English. Culturally localize date/time phrasing (Principle 9).

name: VLM-backed object recognition [ARCH]
shortDesc: [MVP architecture] Use a multimodal vision-language model, not a plain classifier.
description: Architectural MVP flag from the AI Capability Scan. The MVP AI object-recognition feature should call a multimodal VLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini Flash, or GPT-5 mini) rather than a plain image classifier, even for simple use cases. Why: every Phase 2/3 visual feature (spatial narration, cross-modal search, pill ID, ambient display) assumes VLM-grade outputs. Changing vendors later is acceptable; upgrading from classifier to VLM is a full rewrite. Recommended default: Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Gemini Flash fallback. Revisit pricing quarterly.
designNotes: Abstract LLM calls through a single client class. Tag each call with a sensitivity flag so Phase 2 can route sensitive calls on-device without rewriting feature code. Instrument token cost per call from day one.

name: Embeddings-backed semantic search [ARCH]
shortDesc: [MVP architecture] Index via vector embeddings from day one, not keywords.
description: Architectural MVP flag. The Natural Language Search feature should use vector embeddings (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small or Voyage AI) indexed in Firestore vector search or Pinecone. Why: the Phase 2 cross-modal search feature assumes embeddings already exist. Keyword search now + migration later is ~3 days of rework. Embeddings up-front is ~3 days extra now. Same effort, zero migration.
designNotes: Firestore native vector search (released 2024) is the simplest path given existing Firebase stack. Per-patient namespace in embeddings so queries stay local to their own data. Budget: <$1 per patient per month for embedding generation.

name: Spatial context narration
shortDesc: VLM-generated one-line context for each retrieved item.
description: When Margaret searches for her glasses, instead of just a photo, the app returns the photo plus a one-line description: 'kitchen counter, earlier this afternoon, next to the blue bowl.' The VLM reasons about the photo in a single call — location, companion objects, lighting/time cues. Turns a photo into a reconstructible memory, which is the cognitive assist dementia patients most need. Builds on the VLM architectural decision.
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; inspired by Google Ask Photos but corrected for its accuracy issues via structured grounding
designNotes: One VLM call per retrieval (cache the narration). Conservative language — no claims the model can't support. User can correct the narration; corrections feed back as fine-tuning data. Reference: Claude Sonnet 4.6 / Gemini 1.5 Pro.

name: Privacy Mode (on-device inference)
shortDesc: Sensitive queries run entirely on-device via Apple Foundation Models / Gemini Nano / Phi-4.
description: A toggle that routes sensitive content — faces, voice notes, private photos, intimate caregiver observations — through on-device small models (Apple Foundation Models 3B, Gemini Nano 4, Microsoft Phi-4-multimodal, or Llama 3.2). No cloud round-trip. Direct counter to the 'dementia photos in the cloud' trust concern. Major trust signal for Priya and Elena's households.
voicedBy: Anika (CTO); AI Capability Scan; privacy posture from multi-device memo
designNotes: Architectural dependency on the [ARCH] sensitivity-flag abstraction. Gemini Nano 4 or Apple Foundation is the Day 1 target. Fallback to cloud for operations the local model can't handle (with explicit user prompt). Benchmark: sub-500ms latency on target devices.

name: Voice cloning for own-voice reminders
shortDesc: ElevenLabs clones patient's voice; reminders play back in their own voice.
description: Margaret records 'Call the dentist tomorrow' once. The next day, the app plays the reminder back in her own voice, generated via ElevenLabs Instant Voice Cloning ($5/mo starter, 10-sec sample). Hearing yourself says 'this is something I decided to do' in a way a synthetic voice never will — fundamentally different trust dynamic. Enhances the existing Voice Self-Reminders card (Phase 2) by making it an emotional delighter rather than a utility.
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; inspired by competitive analysis gap
designNotes: Explicit two-step consent: recording + use. Revocable. Cloned voice files encrypted at rest, never shared. Audit log of every generation. MVP+ ship only if consent scaffolding is done during MVP.

name: Voice cloning for loved ones (with consent)
shortDesc: Reminders in daughter's voice: "Mom, Priya here, don't forget your pill."
description: Priya records a consent-gated voice sample. Reminders from the app play back in her voice for her mom. 'Mom, it's Tuesday, take your afternoon pill.' The emotional resonance is significantly higher than synthetic voice. Phase 3 because it requires mature consent architecture and explicit two-sided workflow (both Priya and the patient agree to it).
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; extends voice-clone-self to family members
designNotes: Stricter consent than self-cloning: the loved one must explicitly grant the patient use of their voice. Revocable by EITHER party at any time. Never used for emergency or medical claims (framing: 'Priya reminding you' not 'Priya says to take this'). ElevenLabs API.

name: Emotional TTS for morning briefing [UPGRADE]
shortDesc: ElevenLabs v3 / GPT-4o-mini-tts with warm, calm, slow tone.
description: Upgrades the MVP+ Morning Voice Briefing (existing feature) from generic platform TTS to genuinely warm, expressive speech via ElevenLabs Eleven v3 or OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts (both support emotional style prompts like 'calm sympathetic companion'). The emotional quality is what separates 'this is nice' from 'I love this app.' Linda's nervous system feels the difference in the first 3 seconds.
designNotes: User selects from 2-3 curated voices (avoid uncanny valley). Style prompt: 'warm, slow, never chirpy, no false urgency.' Pre-generate the morning briefing at 6am so playback is instant. ElevenLabs or OpenAI TTS; benchmark both.

name: Narrative caregiver digest
shortDesc: LLM summarizes months of mixed-input data into one-paragraph clinical prose.
description: Long-context LLM (Claude Opus 4.6 with 1M context, or Gemini 1.5 Pro) takes months of voice notes, behavioral observations, missed doses, search patterns, and produces a coherent narrative summary in Dr. Patel's preferred format. Different from the Phase 2 trend-charts feature (quantitative) — this is prose Dr. Patel can scan in 90 seconds. Upgrades the Physician Summary Report feature (currently Phase 2) from static to narrative-LLM-driven.
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; Dr. Patel (15-minute appointment reality)
designNotes: Template-guided generation with named sections (cognition, adherence, ADLs, behavior, caregiver observations). Every claim grounded in specific data points with timestamps (no hallucinated events). Clinician can click any sentence to see supporting evidence.

name: Voice-to-structured caregiver log [UPGRADE]
shortDesc: Elena rants; the app extracts strict JSON for the research pipeline.
description: Upgrade to the existing Behavioral Observation Log (Phase 2). Elena voice-dumps 40 seconds about a hard shift. The app (using Claude/GPT/Gemini Structured Outputs, which all hit 99.9% schema compliance) extracts: { time, observation_type, meal_status, item_event, memory_marker, caregiver_mood }. Elena's unstructured speech becomes research-grade data Dr. Carter can aggregate across patients. Three days of engineering.
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; Elena (shift workflow); Dr. Carter (data quality)
designNotes: Schema versioned from day 1. Extraction is a second LLM call after voice-to-text (separate concerns). User can edit any extracted field. Invisible to patient.

name: Cross-modal unified search
shortDesc: One query returns photos + voice notes + caregiver text.
description: Builds on the embeddings architectural decision. Search once; get everything: photos from capture, voice notes Robert left, Elena's shift log entries, Priya's remote annotations. 'What did Robert say about the hearing aids?' returns his voice note AND the photo he took AND Elena's follow-up note. Unifies the information architecture from the user's perspective.
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; Google Ask Photos is the closest reference (but has accuracy issues we'd improve on)
designNotes: CLIP-family embeddings for photo-text alignment + text-text for voice and log data, unified index. Grounding: every search result links to the source artifact (audio timestamp, photo ID). Never synthesize across sources — return matches, let user compose.

name: Bilingual conversation mode
shortDesc: Caregiver speaks English; patient hears Spanish in real-time. Both directions.
description: Real-time voice-to-voice translation (Google Translate Live expanded to iOS March 2026, or Whisper+ElevenLabs chain). Priya video-calls her mom. Priya speaks English; her mom hears Spanish. Her mom speaks Spanish; Priya hears English. Makes the Localization feature dynamic — bridges multigenerational immigrant households that every dementia app we reviewed ignores.
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; builds on Localization (Phase 3)
designNotes: Target: under 1.2s end-to-end latency. Preserve emotional tone (ElevenLabs multilingual does this; Google Translate Live does this). Fallback: caption mode if voice translation fails. Cultural localization of idioms (professional translator review, not raw model output).

name: Adaptive difficulty for Active Recall
shortDesc: AI picks which items to quiz based on historical success + retrieval stage.
description: Enhancement of Scaffolded Active Recall (Phase 2). An adaptive layer picks items at the right difficulty for today — easier items on bad days (cognitive score low per recent retrieval data), harder retrieval on good days. Personalization driven by the retrieval-stage data the feature itself generates. Depends on Active Recall being mature and having accumulated 3-6 months of real retrieval data first.
designNotes: Simple rule-based ramps to start; LLM-driven only after baseline proves clean signal. Never punish failure (Reverse principle). Exposes no difficulty level to patient — the ramping is invisible.

name: Voice distress / emotion trend
shortDesc: Hume AI-powered trend: 'did mom sound anxious this week?'
description: Uses Hume AI's Expression Measurement API (10+ years research, Mount Sinai + Harvard partnerships, Google DeepMind licensing deal Jan 2026) to extract emotional tone from voice input. Graphed as a caregiver-side trend. Risks logged carefully: emotion detection trained on neurotypical speech may mislabel dementia-altered voice patterns. Phase 3+ pending clinical advisor sign-off.
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; Dr. Rosenfeld (needs clinical review)
designNotes: Clinical advisor reviews false-positive rate before ship. Never surfaces raw emotion labels to family ('anxious', 'agitated'); only trend direction and confidence. Opt-in per-patient. Hume pricing: $0.01-0.05 per call.

name: Caregiver admin agent (task execution)
shortDesc: 'Renew mom's prescriptions Tuesday' → agent actually does it.
description: Priya says it; the agent navigates the pharmacy website, authenticates, places the order. Uses Anthropic Claude Computer Use (March 2026 research preview, integrated into Claude Pro/Max) or OpenAI ChatGPT Agent (native agent mode Feb 2026). Major delighter — directly removes caregiver admin overhead. NOT MVP or Phase 2: reliability bar for agentic execution around vulnerable populations + real money + credentials is not yet met.
voicedBy: AI Capability Scan; Priya (caregiver overhead); intentionally deferred
designNotes: Strict scope: pharmacies, grocery delivery, appointment scheduling only. Never banking or credentials-sensitive ops. Always confirms before executing. Revisit Q4 2026 with fresh reliability benchmarks.

name: Predictive risk modeling
shortDesc: Pattern-match against crisis profiles; intervene preventively.
description: Longitudinal usage data plus clinical correlation unlocks predictive models: "In the 2 weeks before a crisis, patients in our cohort showed X pattern." Enables caregivers to intervene before emergencies. Far horizon — requires both the data and the research validation to be credible.
designNotes: Ethical minefield — requires clear framing (support, not surveillance). Likely gated by clinical advisor. Possible regulatory classification as decision support.

name: Cloud sync hardening
shortDesc: Offline-first, conflict resolution, spotty-connectivity tolerance.
description: MVP ships multi-device with basic Firestore sync. Phase 2 hardens it: offline-first queue beyond single optimistic writes, conflict resolution for simultaneous edits, smarter retries. Without this, users on spotty connections (Priya on transit Wi-Fi) experience data loss.
designNotes: Implement a proper write-ahead log. Last-write-wins is acceptable for most fields; photos/text notes need merge. Testing against airplane-mode toggling.

name: Configurable notification levels
shortDesc: From real-time everything (Daniel) to emergency-only (Susan).
description: Daniel wants to know every time his dad takes a pill. Susan wants to be left alone unless her mom is in danger. A single notification setting is impossible — the design must accommodate radically different engagement levels per family member. Configurable at MVP+ if easy, Phase 2 if not.
designNotes: Four presets: Real-time / Daily digest / Weekly digest / Emergency only. Per-family-member, not per-household. Changeable without patient awareness.

name: Trend dashboards
shortDesc: Week-over-week search patterns, medication adherence trends.
description: Priya's retention driver. Daily check-ins get old; weekly trends tell her something meaningful. Charts of search frequency, common queries, medication adherence, caregiver-logged incidents. Not for the patient — for the remote family's mental model.
designNotes: Meaningful charts only — no vanity metrics. Highlight changes, not absolute numbers. Plain-language annotations ("Mom searched 'keys' 3× more this week than last").

name: Physician summary report
shortDesc: One-page, traffic-light, print-friendly for 15-min appointments.
description: Dr. Patel has 15 minutes with this patient every 6 months. A one-page report — green/yellow/red on cognition, adherence, ADLs — that he can scan in 60 seconds is an adoption multiplier. Build exactly what Dr. Patel asks for, no more. This is the PCP's 15-minute-appointment hook.
designNotes: Print-optimized PDF. Traffic-light summary at top; supporting detail below. Generatable on demand by caregiver. Never auto-send without explicit action.

name: Routine sequencing
shortDesc: Visual step-by-step: brush teeth → dress → meds → breakfast.
description: James can't remember what comes next. A visual sequence — photo-step-photo-step — guides him through his morning routine. OT-validated approach. Caregiver sets up once; patient uses daily. Different from full ADL mapping — this is just "what's next."
designNotes: Max 6 steps per routine. Photos over text. Patient can skip forward/backward. No shame messaging on skipped steps.

name: Behavioral observation log
shortDesc: Quick voice-note log for caregivers during shifts.
description: Elena observes "patient seemed more confused around 3pm; refused lunch." Instead of paper notes or a separate app, she speaks it into ReCall. Voice-first because typing during a shift is impractical. Feeds into caregiver handoff summaries. Professional-caregiver adoption driver.
designNotes: Voice-to-text with caregiver-only visibility. Timestamped. Aggregated into daily/shift summaries. Never surfaced to patient.

name: Daily status accuracy
shortDesc: How reliably the green/yellow/red reflects reality.
description: The caregiver status view is only trusted if it's accurate. False alarms burn out family; false reassurance is dangerous. Phase 2 work hardens the signal: thresholds tuned from real data, context-aware (travel, visitors), and transparent about what it's measuring.
designNotes: Track false-positive and false-negative rates. Caregiver can configure thresholds. Log what triggered the status so caregiver can trace it.

name: Structured data export (CSV/JSON)
shortDesc: Timestamp, query, category, result — exportable for research.
description: Patient and family don't care. Dr. Carter cares profoundly — this is how ReCall becomes a research tool. Timestamp + query + category + result + outcome, exportable as CSV or JSON. Required for any academic collaboration.
designNotes: Anonymizable. Consent-gated. Periodic export (weekly) rather than real-time. Schema documented publicly.

name: ADL decline mapping
shortDesc: Which daily-living activities are failing, in what order.
description: Occupational therapists and neurologists use this to stage progression. Patient/family don't see it. Based on search patterns and caregiver notes, ReCall can produce a clinician-readable progression map.
designNotes: Clinician-only view. Maps to standard ADL taxonomies (Katz, Lawton IADL).

name: Research consent flow
shortDesc: Opt-in flow for anonymized data to support research studies.
description: Required to use any of the data for research. Architecturally a simple flow (opt-in checkbox + data-use explanation), but legally and procedurally needs an IRB template and a clinical advisor. Build it early, leverage it long.
designNotes: Written at 8th-grade reading level. Revocable at any time. Separate consent for passive usage data vs. photos.

name: Multi-patient dashboard
shortDesc: Facility manager view: 30+ patients at a glance.
description: Karen runs a facility with 30 residents across 3 shifts. A dashboard view — patients as cards, color-coded by status — lets her prioritize. Not a consumer feature; an institutional-market feature. Phase 3 because it requires role-based access, bulk onboarding, and HIPAA architecture.
designNotes: Built on top of the caregiver status view but multiplexed. Bulk actions for shift handoff. Never exposes patient-level detail without role check.

name: Bulk patient onboarding
shortDesc: CSV/upload-based onboarding for facility intake.
description: Facility admissions adds 3-5 patients a week. Individual-signup flow is too slow. Bulk CSV import plus device-pairing QR codes. Institutional-market gate.
designNotes: Spreadsheet template. Role-based default configs. QR-code device pairing reduces onboarding to 30 seconds per patient.

name: HIPAA compliance framework
shortDesc: BAA-eligible hosting, audit trails, breach procedures.
description: Required to serve any institutional customer. MVP can stay pre-HIPAA (architectural posture, not legal coverage), but Phase 3 signing a BAA with Firebase, writing access controls, and formalizing breach procedures is the gating item for facility sales.
designNotes: Firebase BAA-eligible tier. Audit logs for every admin action. Data residency options (US-only, EU-only) for multi-region customers.

name: Cognitive exercise framework
shortDesc: OT-assigned practice tasks with configurable assistance.
description: Dr. Lauren assigns specific practice exercises. The app presents them at the right time with a configurable amount of help (full assistance, partial, none). This is the Active-Recall feature's clinical big brother — a full therapeutic protocol, not just a retrieval toggle.
designNotes: Requires OT-approved exercise library. Clinician assigns via a prescriber-side view. Patient sees exercises as part of their daily flow, not as a separate mode.

name: API access
shortDesc: Programmatic access for researchers and power users.
description: Daniel (over-involved son) would love an API. So would any research partner. Not a priority — maybe 1% of users would touch it. Build only if it unlocks a meaningful research partnership or enterprise contract.
designNotes: Read-only for V1. OAuth. Rate-limited. Scope-limited (no photo access without explicit user consent per-request).

name: Wearable integration
shortDesc: Apple Watch, Galaxy Ring — passive health signals.
description: Sleep, heart rate, activity. Feeds caregiver status and research data. Only relevant for patients already wearing a device; Margaret (our MVP target) may not. Useful as a data multiplier, not a primary feature.
designNotes: Optional. Never required for core features. Opt-in explicit. Not a competitive focus — big tech will out-build this.

name: GPS / location tracking
shortDesc: Some users want it; patient feels surveilled.
description: Daniel (over-involved son) and Priya (remote) want always-on location. Patients feel surveilled and lose trust. Never in the primary patient experience. Phase 2+ opt-in for family use only, framed as safety (wandering alerts) not tracking. Never visible to patient.
designNotes: Opt-in by family via configuration. Geofence-based alerts only, not continuous logs. Patient sees nothing in their UI about location sharing.

name: Real-time activity alerts
shortDesc: Daniel wants all of them; Susan is burned out on notifications.
description: The same feature is a Performance driver for Daniel and a Reverse item for Susan. Solution: make configurable (see Configurable notifications, Phase 2). Never default to real-time. Flagged here as Reverse to remember the risk of over-indexing on power users.
designNotes: Default: daily digest. Opt-in for real-time. Never push during quiet hours (user-configurable).

name: Full activity log (patient-facing)
shortDesc: Users don't want to see a log of their own dementia.
description: A raw log of every search, every forgotten item, every repeated query is devastating to read. Margaret doesn't want to see "you asked 23 times today." Admin-surface-only. Never in patient-facing UI. This is a Reverse feature disguised as a Performance feature — reject it.
designNotes: Admin/caregiver view only. Never summarized back to patient. Engineering: still log the data; just never render it to patient.

name: "Good job!" praise messages
shortDesc: Margaret was a librarian for 30 years. Never patronize her.
description: Well-meaning designers add "Great job remembering!" Praise. Don't. Margaret finds it patronizing. Use neutral factual language always: "Photo saved" not "Good job photographing!" This is Principle 10 (treat users as adults) as a specific product constraint.
designNotes: Copy review requirement: every string audited for condescension. No exclamation points on success events. Neutral acknowledgements only.

name: Facial recognition
shortDesc: Dementia + face ID is a privacy minefield. Phase 3+ only.
description: Margaret (patient) and Daniel (family) both want it for obvious use cases. Privacy advocates, elder-law attorneys, and regulators will push back hard. Manual tagging in V1; facial recognition only in Phase 3+ with explicit consent workflow, clinical advisor sign-off, and documented opt-out.
designNotes: Opt-in. Patient-controlled. Never on-by-default. Face templates stored locally where possible. Separate consent from general terms.

name: Gamification / streaks
shortDesc: Lauren (OT) wants streaks for therapy; patients reject them as gamey.
description: Streaks, scores, and "you're on a 5-day streak!" messages are motivational in a fitness app and disastrous for a dementia patient who will eventually break the streak — and then blame themselves. Clinical-mode ONLY (gated behind a therapist prescriber). Never in consumer mode.
designNotes: Gated behind clinician-assigned mode. Breakable-streak pattern explicitly avoided (no "you broke your streak" messaging ever).

name: Password storage
shortDesc: Real need (Margaret, Priya) but wrong time (Anika says no).
description: Margaret gets locked out of email weekly. The password notebook is lost. Priya is furious. BUT — storing credentials for a vulnerable population without a security architecture review is liability we can't absorb in MVP. Defer until Phase 3+ with a dedicated security pass and possibly third-party integration.
designNotes: Possible integration with 1Password Families or similar rather than custom vault. Never MVP. Never without security review.

name: Caregiver job monitoring
shortDesc: Families want oversight of paid caregivers; caregivers feel surveilled.
description: Daniel wants time-in-home, task completion, voice logs from Elena's shift. Elena feels surveilled; Karen (facility manager) is uncomfortable; union/labor implications in some states. Reframe as care-quality signals, not surveillance. Requires careful product language — this is not a feature to add, it's a framing question.
designNotes: NEVER market as monitoring. Frame as "shift notes and continuity." Visible to caregiver that the data exists. Opt-in by caregiver.

name: Low-touch family mode
shortDesc: Emergency-only mode for burned-out family (Susan).
description: Susan is burned out. She will delete the app if it sends her a notification a week. She needs a mode that says: "We'll only contact you if something is actually wrong." Labeled Reverse because forcing this mode on Daniel would make him rage-quit — it MUST be opt-in per family member.
designNotes: Clear opt-in flow. User sees explicitly what qualifies as "wrong" (medication missed 24h, safety check red, caregiver alert). Reversible at any time.
